lesson.title: Expecting the Unexpected: The Try-Except Block
lesson.summary: The try-except block lets a program attempt code that might fail and respond on its own terms instead of crashing with an unhandled exception.
lesson.body:
Up to now, an exception like IndexError or KeyError has meant the program stops immediately and prints a traceback, what is called an unhandled exception. That is fine while learning, but it is rarely what a real program should do. A grading tool should not shut down entirely just because one lookup failed. Python gives you a way to anticipate specific failures ahead of time and keep the program running anyway: the try-except block.

The idea is straightforward. Code that might raise an exception goes inside a try block. Code that should run only if a specific exception actually occurs goes inside an except block naming that exception type. If nothing goes wrong, the except block is skipped entirely and execution continues normally right after it.

```python
def average(numbers):
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

try:
    print(average([]))
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Can't average an empty list.")
```

Inside average([]), sum([]) is 0 and len([]) is 0, so the function attempts 0 / 0, which raises ZeroDivisionError before it ever gets a chance to return a value. Because that call sits inside the try block, Python does not crash the whole program. It jumps straight to the except ZeroDivisionError block, which matches, and runs that instead. Output:

```
Can't average an empty list.
```

Nothing about print(average([])) actually finishes normally, the exception cuts it off partway through, but the program keeps going because the except block caught it and handled it.

The except clause names a specific exception type on purpose. If the code inside try had raised some other kind of exception instead, say a TypeError from passing in something that is not a list of numbers at all, this particular except block would not match it, and that other exception would propagate upward unhandled, exactly as if there were no try block there at all. A try-except block only protects against the exception types it explicitly names. That specificity is exactly what the next lesson builds on, since a single try block is often guarding against more than one thing that could go wrong at once.
